animals.blurb: Introduced from Europe, these familiar snails are considered pests in gardens but are also the escargot of French cuisine. They seal themselves in their shells during dry periods.
animals.hint: A garden pest that's also French cuisine

animals.blurb: North America's second-largest slug, reaching 10 inches. Their bright yellow color makes them forest floor icons of the Pacific Northwest. They play an important role recycling nutrients.
animals.hint: A giant yellow forest recycler of the Pacific

animals.blurb: A large European slug now common in North America, recognized by leopard-like spots. They have a bizarre mating ritual where pairs dangle from mucus threads while intertwined.
animals.hint: A spotted slug with an acrobatic mating dance

animals.blurb: Ecosystem engineers that build massive reefs and filter up to 50 gallons of water daily. Once so abundant they created navigation hazards, they are now recovering through restoration efforts.
animals.hint: A reef-building filter that cleans 50 gallons daily

animals.blurb: Common on both coasts, blue mussels attach to surfaces with tough protein threads called byssal threads. Scientists study these threads to develop underwater adhesives.
animals.hint: A shore-clinging shellfish with super-strong glue

animals.blurb: Unlike most bivalves, scallops can swim by clapping their shells together. They have up to 100 brilliant blue eyes along their shell edges that detect movement and shadows.
animals.hint: A swimming shellfish with dozens of blue eyes

animals.blurb: The largest octopus species, with arm spans reaching 20 feet. Highly intelligent, they can solve puzzles, recognize individual humans, and escape from almost any container.
animals.hint: A massive, intelligent puzzle-solver of the deep

animals.blurb: A master of camouflage that can change color, texture, and pattern in milliseconds. Primarily nocturnal, they hunt crabs and small fish on Caribbean reefs.
animals.hint: A color-changing reef hunter that hides in plain sight

animals.blurb: These small squid gather in massive spawning aggregations that attract whales, sea lions, and seabirds. They live fast—only 6-9 months—and die after spawning.
animals.hint: A short-lived squid that spawns in massive gatherings

animals.blurb: Large predatory sea snails that pry open clams and oysters with their muscular foot. Their egg cases wash up on beaches as strange spiral chains called 'mermaid's necklaces.'
animals.hint: A clam-prying snail that leaves mermaid's necklaces
